notes: AC15's primary canary fixture. must_not_fire CSC-AAA-0010: its catalogue title is 'Local user at privilege 15 with a type 0 or type 7 password' and its rationale names exactly those two encryption types; this fixture's privilege-15 user (`username admin privilege 15 secret 9 $9$CANARY0001`) uses type 9 (scrypt), a strong KDF, not type 0 or 7 -- the rule correctly does not fire. The masker must preserve the readable type marker so a reader can see this, but that is separate from whether CSC-AAA-0010 itself fires on this line. must_not_fire CSC-SNMP-0002/0004: every `snmp-server community` line in this fixture is `RO` (never `RW`) and carries an ACL clause (`RO 99`, the fixture's frozen worked-line spelling for the extent-preservation test) -- CSC-SNMP-0002's catalogue title is 'Community string is read-write (RW)' (test_kind `value`, an RO line cannot match it) and CSC-SNMP-0004's is 'Community string not restricted by an ACL' (test_kind `absent`, an ACL clause -- even one naming an undefined ACL, which is CSC-SNMP-0005's separate, already-firing concern -- is present, so this check's own absence condition is not met). Both correctly do not fire: the extent-preservation lines exist so *some* check can read the RO/99 values, not to make CSC-SNMP-0002/0004 fire, and the fixture's actual content (RO, not RW) never satisfies those checks' catalogue conditions. This is real, correct rule behaviour, not a rule defect. This manifest is consulted by test_corpus.py; the canary/secret-value assertions themselves live in test_masking_invariant.py, and test_corpus.py also asserts directly that no finding's evidence.text carries a raw canary value.
